## Overview

Can a decision model find defects in images of manufactured parts when it
sees only a few reference images? And are its probabilities calibrated, so
that a probability of 0.8 means that about 8 of 10 such parts are defective?

This vignette examines these questions with the package, on five datasets of
industrial images. It repeats the steps of a study of decision models on
these images (the original study; its record is public at
<https://fmegahed.github.io/decision-models-for-industrial-image-qc/>). It
tunes the descriptions of the answers, chooses the number of reference images
and the image size, fits a calibrator, and saves each setup for one final
test. It uses three models:

* Jev, from TypeSafe, with `decider_typesafe()`. The version is pinned to
  `jev-1.14.0`, so a later version of Jev does not change the results.
* gpt-6-luna, on the Decisions API of OpenAI, with `decider_openai()`.
* Clef-Flash, from Cloudflare, on a local SGLang server, with
  `decider_systemone()`.

The results below come from live calls on `r knitr::combine_words(run_dates)`. The
package saved them in `inst/extdata/study_again.rds`, so this vignette builds
without a key, a network or the images. The script `data-raw/study_again.R`
in the source of the package made them. Its code is the code of this
vignette.

## Data

The five datasets come from a published study of image inspection with CLIP
(Megahed et al., 2026). Each image is `nominal` (a good part) or `defective`.

| Dataset | Images | Nominal | Defective |
|---|---|---|---|
| `extrusion` | Frames of the extrusion profile of a 3D printer | `normal` | `over`, `under` (too much or too little material) |
| `microstructure` | Simulated microstructure images (EBSD) | `Uniform` | `Band`, `Bimodal`, `SingleCrystal`, each at a `low`, `medium` or `high` level |
| `pan_images` | Surfaces of metallic pans | `nominal` | `defective` |
| `pipe_staple` | A pipe staple on a car production line | `good` | `missing` (the staple is missing) |
| `textiles` | Simulated textured surfaces | `nominal` | `local` (a small flaw), `global` (a change of the whole texture) |

The authors of Megahed et al. (2026) recorded the extrusion images and
simulated the microstructure images. The pan images come from Megahed and
Camelio (2012). The authors simulated the textile images with the R package
spc4sts (Bui & Apley, 2021). The pipe staple images come
from the Automotive Visual Inspection Dataset (AutoVI) of Renault (Carvalho et
al., 2024).

### Licences

The images are in the public repository
[fmegahed/qe_genai](https://github.com/fmegahed/qe_genai), folder `data/`,
under the MIT licence. The pipe staple images keep the licence of AutoVI,
CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: give credit, use them for non-commercial work only, and share
changed images under the same licence. The table `study_sets.csv` of the
package holds only the image names and the labels. The package holds no
image of these datasets, except the 50 textile images of
`vignette("images")`. Here they are learning or reference images, not test
images.

### Images

Download the repository (about 360 MB):

```{bash clone, eval = FALSE}
git clone https://github.com/fmegahed/qe_genai.git
```

Then tell R where the images are, and where the state files and the setups
go:

```{r paths}
image_dir <- "qe_genai/data"
state_dir <- "state"
setup_dir <- "setups"
```

```{r folders, eval = FALSE}
dir.create(state_dir)
dir.create(setup_dir)
```

## Rows

The table `study_sets.csv` gives each image one role. The image paths are
relative to the folder `data/` of fmegahed/qe_genai.

```{r sets, script = TRUE}
sets <- system.file("extdata", "study_sets.csv", package = "decisions") |>
  utils::read.csv() |>
  tibble::as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    truth = factor(
      dplyr::if_else(class == "nominal", "normal", "defective"),
      levels = c("normal", "defective")
    ),
    path = file.path(image_dir, image_path)
  )

by_dataset <- split(sets, sets$dataset)

table(sets$dataset, sets$role)
```

The roles:

* `learning`: labeled images to tune on. The tuning steps choose the
  descriptions and the image settings on these images.
* `reference`: four images per class, with a `rank` from 1 to 4. A setup with
  `k` references per class uses the ranks 1 to `k`. The references come from
  the learning images. No step scores the references that its setup uses.
* `calibration`: labeled images to fit the calibrator on. The pans have too
  few images for this role. For the pans, the calibrator uses the learning
  images and the references that the chosen setup does not use.
* `test`: the images for the final estimate. They are scored one time only.

Each step of the tuning looks at the scores and keeps the better choice. A
choice that looks better on the images that it was chosen on is, on average,
less good on new images. So the estimate of a tuned setup on its own learning
images is too high. The test images give an honest estimate only if no choice
used them. So the test images are scored one time, at the end, after all
choices are fixed. `score_setup()` refuses rows with the role `test`, and
`evaluate_once()` scores them one time (see "Test").

The original study drew the rows once, with fixed seeds.

## Question

Each dataset gets the same choice question, with two answers. The
instructions name `inspection_image`: that is the name of the input image in
each request. The descriptions of the answers change during the tuning. The
first candidate of each dataset is a generic description.

```{r question, script = TRUE}
quality_question <- function(descriptions) {
  list(quality = question_choice(
    "Inspect `inspection_image` for manufacturing defects. Select exactly one category.",
    descriptions
  ))
}

generic <- c(
  normal = "No visible manufacturing defects; the part appears conforming.",
  defective = "At least one visible manufacturing defect or anomaly."
)
```

## Models

```{r deciders, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
deciders <- list(
  jev = decider_typesafe("jev-1.14.0"),
  openai = decider_openai("gpt-6-luna"),
  clef = decider_systemone(
    "http://localhost:30000", "Cloudflare/clef-flash", image_format = "images"
  )
)
```

`decider_typesafe()` reads the key from the environment variable
`TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, and `decider_openai()` from `OPENAI_API_KEY` (for
example, in `~/.Renviron`). Clef-Flash runs on your computer, on a GPU, and
needs no key. The shell command below starts its server with Docker
(`vignette("images")` has the details). It is not run here.

```{bash clef-server, eval = FALSE}
docker run --gpus all --shm-size 8g --ipc=host -p 30000:30000 \
  lmsysorg/sglang:dev-clef \
  sglang serve --model-path Cloudflare/clef-flash --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000
```

The code below runs one model at a time. `model_name` is `"jev"`, `"openai"`
or `"clef"`.

```{r model-name, eval = FALSE}
model_name <- "jev"
```

## Setups

A setup holds one complete decision: the decider, the question with its
descriptions, the reference images and the image settings.
`make_setup()` makes the setup of one model and dataset with `k` references
per class. `upscale = TRUE` enlarges each image to `max_size` pixels on its
longest side: TypeSafe refuses images under 280 pixels, and some images of
these datasets are smaller.

`score_rows()` scores a setup on labeled rows with `score_setup()`. It gives
`score_setup()` the role of each row, so a test row stops the call before any
request. A reference row counts as a learning row. Each run keeps its answers
in a state file (`path`): a run that stops continues and does not pay twice.
`score_rows()` also keeps the image paths with the result, so a later step
can check that its rows are in the same order as the saved answers.

```{r setup-functions, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
make_setup <- function(model, dataset, descriptions, k, max_size) {
  references <- by_dataset[[dataset]] |>
    dplyr::filter(role == "reference", rank <= k) |>
    dplyr::arrange(rank)
  decision_setup(
    deciders[[model]], quality_question(descriptions),
    references = list(
      normal = references$path[references$truth == "normal"],
      defective = references$path[references$truth == "defective"]
    ),
    max_size = max_size, upscale = TRUE
  )
}

score_rows <- function(setup, rows, path) {
  score_setup(
    setup, image = rows$path, truth = rows$truth,
    role = dplyr::if_else(rows$role == "reference", "learning", rows$role),
    path = path
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(image_path = list(rows$image_path))
}

state_file <- function(...) {
  file.path(state_dir, paste0(paste(..., sep = "_"), ".json"))
}
```

## Wording

### Candidates

The candidate descriptions come from description loops. In each loop, an
agent (Claude Code) looked at 96 labeled images of one dataset (the learning
images and the references of rank 3 and 4), in a sandbox folder that it could
not leave. The image names gave no label.
It wrote one candidate at a time: a new text for `normal` and for
`defective`, from the images that the best candidate so far scored badly. A
script scored each candidate, with two references per class, and gave the
agent the ROC AUC. A loop had at most 6 candidates, and candidate 1 was the
generic description.

The loops for Jev and Clef-Flash ran in the original study. gpt-6-luna got its
own loops, with the same rules, scored with `score_setup()` of this package.
The pans have no loop: they keep the generic description. The page
[description loops](https://fmegahed.github.io/decision-models-for-industrial-image-qc/pages/description_loops.html)
of the study record shows each candidate of the study loops with the reason
for the change.

The saved results hold the candidates of all loops:

```{r candidates, eval = FALSE}
saved <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "study_again.rds", package = "decisions"))
candidates <- dplyr::select(
  saved$wording, model, dataset, candidate, normal, defective, reason
)
```

### Keep rule

Two wordings can get a different AUC by chance alone: 96 images give a
rough AUC. If each higher AUC replaced the best wording, the loop would follow
this noise, and it would keep the wording that fits these 96 images by luck.
The keep rule protects against this. A candidate replaces the current best
only if its AUC is at least 0.02 higher. Candidate 1 is the first best.

```{r keep-rule, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
keep_rule <- function(auc, gain = 0.02) {
  best <- purrr::accumulate(auc, \(best, x) {
    if (round(x - best, 10) >= gain) x else best
  })
  c(TRUE, diff(best) > 0)
}
```

`round()` removes the small errors of floating-point numbers, so a gain of
exactly 0.02 counts.

### Scores

The wording step scores the candidates of each loop in their order, on the
same 96 images, with two references per class and `max_size = 768`. For Jev
and Clef-Flash, these are new calls with the package. For gpt-6-luna, its
loop already scored its candidates in this way, so its AUCs come from its
loop logs, with no new call.

```{r wording-setups, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
score_candidate <- function(model, dataset, candidate, normal, defective) {
  setup <- make_setup(
    model, dataset, c(normal = normal, defective = defective),
    k = 2, max_size = 768
  )
  design <- dplyr::filter(
    by_dataset[[dataset]],
    role == "learning" | (role == "reference" & rank > 2)
  )
  score_rows(setup, design, state_file("wording", model, dataset, candidate))
}

wording <- dplyr::filter(candidates, model == model_name)
```

```{r wording-score, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
wording <- wording |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    result = purrr::pmap(
      list(model, dataset, candidate, normal, defective), score_candidate
    ),
    auc = purrr::map_dbl(result, "estimate")
  )
```

The keep rule then gives the final wording of each dataset. The pans get the
generic description.

```{r wording-keep, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
wording <- dplyr::mutate(wording, kept = keep_rule(auc), .by = dataset)

final_wording <- wording |>
  dplyr::filter(kept) |>
  dplyr::slice_tail(n = 1, by = dataset) |>
  dplyr::select(model, dataset, normal, defective) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble::tibble(
    model = model_name, dataset = "pan_images",
    normal = generic[["normal"]], defective = generic[["defective"]]
  ))
```

The table gives, for each model and dataset, the number of candidates, the
AUC of the generic description (candidate 1), the final candidate and its
AUC.

```{r wording-table, echo = FALSE}
show(wording_summary)
```

```{r wording-facts, include = FALSE}
gain <- wording_summary |>
  dplyr::mutate(gain = final_auc - generic_auc) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(gain))
generic_only <- dplyr::filter(wording_summary, candidates == 1)
generic_kept <- dplyr::filter(wording_summary, candidates > 1, final == 1)
clef_textiles <- pick(saved$wording, "clef", "textiles")
held_back <- dplyr::filter(
  clef_textiles, !kept, auc == max(clef_textiles$auc[!clef_textiles$kept])
)
kept_one <- dplyr::filter(clef_textiles, kept) |> dplyr::slice_tail(n = 1)
```

The loops raised the AUC of the generic description on most datasets. The
largest gains: `r knitr::combine_words(paste0(model_label[gain$model[1:3]], " on the ", dataset_label[gain$dataset[1:3]], " (", fmt(gain$generic_auc[1:3]), " to ", fmt(gain$final_auc[1:3]), ")"))`.
For `r name_setups(generic_only)`, the study loop stopped after the generic
description. For `r name_setups(generic_kept)`, no candidate beat the generic
description (`r fmt(generic_kept$generic_auc)`).

The keep rule worked as intended. For Clef-Flash on the textiles, candidate
`r kept_one$candidate` scored `r fmt(kept_one$auc, 3)` and candidate
`r held_back$candidate` scored `r fmt(held_back$auc, 3)`. The gain of
`r fmt(held_back$auc - kept_one$auc, 3)` is less than 0.02, so candidate
`r kept_one$candidate` stayed the final wording.

These AUCs are on the images that the loops chose on, so they are too high
(see "Rows"). The calibration and test images give fresher estimates.

The final descriptions of the textiles. Each model has its own loop, so each
model has its own wording:

```{r textiles-wording, echo = FALSE}
saved$chosen |>
  dplyr::filter(dataset == "textiles") |>
  dplyr::select(model, normal, defective) |>
  show()
```

## Grid

The grid tries 6 setups for each model and dataset: `k` = 1, 2 or 4
references per class, and `max_size` = 512 or 768 pixels. Each setup uses the
final wording. It scores the learning images that are not references: 92 per
dataset, and 12 for the pans. The setup with the highest AUC is the chosen
setup. A tie goes to the smaller `k`, then to the smaller size.

```{r grid-setups, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
score_grid <- function(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size) {
  setup <- make_setup(
    model, dataset, c(normal = normal, defective = defective), k, max_size
  )
  learning <- dplyr::filter(by_dataset[[dataset]], role == "learning")
  score_rows(setup, learning, state_file("grid", model, dataset, k, max_size))
}

grid <- final_wording |>
  dplyr::cross_join(tibble::tibble(
    k = rep(c(1, 2, 4), each = 2), max_size = rep(c(512, 768), times = 3)
  ))
```

```{r grid-score, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
grid <- grid |>
  dplyr::mutate(result = purrr::pmap(
    list(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size), score_grid
  ))
```

```{r grid-choose, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
grid <- dplyr::bind_cols(
  dplyr::select(grid, -result),
  purrr::list_rbind(grid$result) |>
    dplyr::select(-metric) |>
    dplyr::rename(auc = estimate)
)

chosen <- grid |>
  dplyr::arrange(dataset, dplyr::desc(round(auc, 10)), k, max_size) |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 1, by = dataset)
```

The AUC of each setup:

```{r grid-table, echo = FALSE}
saved$grid |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    `k 1, 512` = auc[k == 1 & max_size == 512],
    `k 1, 768` = auc[k == 1 & max_size == 768],
    `k 2, 512` = auc[k == 2 & max_size == 512],
    `k 2, 768` = auc[k == 2 & max_size == 768],
    `k 4, 512` = auc[k == 4 & max_size == 512],
    `k 4, 768` = auc[k == 4 & max_size == 768],
    .by = c(model, dataset)
  ) |>
  show()
```

The chosen setups:

```{r chosen-table, echo = FALSE}
saved$chosen |>
  dplyr::select(model, dataset, k, max_size, auc) |>
  show()
```

```{r grid-facts, include = FALSE}
chosen_k <- \(model_name, dataset_name) pick(saved$chosen, model_name, dataset_name)$k
token_ratio <- saved$grid |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    ratio = input_tokens[max_size == 512] / input_tokens[max_size == 768],
    .by = c(model, dataset, k)
  )
perfect <- dplyr::filter(saved$grid, round(auc, 10) == 1)
```

No setting is the best for all models and datasets. On the extrusion images,
the chosen setups use `k` = `r chosen_k("jev", "extrusion")` (Jev),
`r chosen_k("openai", "extrusion")` (gpt-6-luna) and
`r chosen_k("clef", "extrusion")` (Clef-Flash). On the microstructures, they
use `k` = `r chosen_k("jev", "microstructure")`,
`r chosen_k("openai", "microstructure")` and
`r chosen_k("clef", "microstructure")`. Images of 512 pixels need about
`r round(100 * mean(token_ratio$ratio))` % of the input tokens of images of
768 pixels, and they were often as good. `r nrow(perfect)` of the
`r nrow(saved$grid)` setups reach an AUC of 1, all on the
`r knitr::combine_words(dataset_label[unique(perfect$dataset)])`. The tie rule
then picks the setup with the fewest references. On the 12 learning images of
the pans, an AUC of 1 says little.

These AUCs are on the images that the grid chose on, so they are too high
(see "Rows"). The calibration and test images give fresher estimates.

## Calibration

A calibrator corrects the probabilities of a model, so that they agree with
the rates of defects. This vignette uses Platt scaling: a logistic
regression of the truth on the logit of the probability of `defective`. It
is fitted on the calibration images, with the chosen setup.

```{r calibration-setups, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
calibration_rows <- function(dataset, k) {
  rows <- by_dataset[[dataset]]
  if (dataset == "pan_images") {
    dplyr::filter(rows, role == "learning" | (role == "reference" & rank > k))
  } else {
    dplyr::filter(rows, role == "calibration")
  }
}

score_calibration <- function(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size) {
  setup <- make_setup(
    model, dataset, c(normal = normal, defective = defective), k, max_size
  )
  rows <- calibration_rows(dataset, k)
  score_rows(setup, rows, state_file("calibration", model, dataset, k, max_size))
}

calibration <- dplyr::select(chosen, model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size)
```

```{r calibration-score, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
calibration <- calibration |>
  dplyr::mutate(result = purrr::pmap(
    list(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size), score_calibration
  ))
```

```{r platt-facts, include = FALSE}
logistic_warned <- dplyr::filter(saved$platt, logistic_warning)
logistic_saturated <- dplyr::filter(saved$platt, logistic_saturated)
stopifnot(all(paste(logistic_warned$model, logistic_warned$dataset) %in%
  paste(logistic_saturated$model, logistic_saturated$dataset)))
sci <-\(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
separated <- dplyr::filter(calibration_wide, round(auc, 10) == 1)
worse <- dplyr::filter(
  calibration_wide, brier_after > brier_before | log_loss_after > log_loss_before
)
steep <- dplyr::filter(saved$platt, lowest < 1e-12 | 1 - highest < 1e-12)
steepest <- dplyr::slice_max(saved$platt, slope, n = 1)
near_bounds <- sum(saved$platt$near_bounds)
auc_same <- isTRUE(all.equal(calibration_wide$auc, calibration_wide$auc_after))
auc_changed <- dplyr::filter(calibration_wide, abs(auc - auc_after) > 1e-12)
grid_auc <- \(model_name, dataset_name) pick(saved$chosen, model_name, dataset_name)$auc
calibration_auc <- \(model_name, dataset_name) pick(calibration_wide, model_name, dataset_name)$auc
```

Platt scaling does not fit the labels 0 and 1. With N+ defective and N- normal
calibration images, its target is (N+ + 1) / (N+ + 2) for a defective image
and 1 / (N- + 2) for a normal image. These targets keep the fit finite when a
model ranks the few calibration images almost perfectly. A fit on the labels
0 and 1 then has no finite solution: its slope grows without limit, and the
calibrated probabilities become 0 or 1. The logistic calibrator of probably
(`probably::cal_estimate_logistic()` with `smooth = FALSE`) fits the labels 0
and 1, so it saturates on so few, almost perfectly ranked calibration images.
On the calibration images of this vignette, its `glm()` warns for
`r nrow(logistic_warned)` of the `r nrow(saved$platt)` setups, and its
calibrated probabilities come within 1e-12 of 0 or 1 for
`r nrow(logistic_saturated)` setups. The calibrators of probably fit well
with more calibration images. The targets are not 0 or 1, so the fit uses
`family = quasibinomial`. `clip()` keeps each probability between 0.005 and
0.995, the clamp of the original study, so that its logit stays between about
-5.3 and 5.3.

```{r calibration-fit, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
clip <- function(prob) pmin(pmax(prob, 0.005), 0.995)

platt_fit <- function(prob, truth) {
  n_defective <- sum(truth == "defective")
  n_normal <- sum(truth == "normal")
  target <- dplyr::if_else(
    truth == "defective", (n_defective + 1) / (n_defective + 2), 1 / (n_normal + 2)
  )
  stats::glm(target ~ stats::qlogis(clip(prob)), family = stats::quasibinomial())
}

platt_apply <- function(prob, intercept, slope) {
  stats::plogis(intercept + slope * stats::qlogis(clip(prob)))
}
```

`platt_row()` fits the Platt scaling of one setup and keeps its two
coefficients and the class counts.

```{r calibration-platt, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
platt_row <- function(model, dataset, k, result, ...) {
  truth <- calibration_rows(dataset, k)$truth
  fit <- platt_fit(result$answers[[1]]$.pred_defective, truth)
  tibble::tibble(
    model = model, dataset = dataset,
    n_normal = sum(truth == "normal"), n_defective = sum(truth == "defective"),
    intercept = stats::coef(fit)[[1]], slope = stats::coef(fit)[[2]]
  )
}

platt <- calibration |>
  purrr::pmap(platt_row) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
```

The setups keep no calibrator. `write_setup()` saves each setup as one JSON
file, and the Platt fits stay in the saved results. So `evaluate_once()`
scores the raw probabilities, and `platt_apply()` maps them to calibrated
ones. (A setup can hold a probably calibrator, with `decision_setup(...,
calibrator = )`, when there are enough calibration images for it.)

```{r calibration-write, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
calibration |>
  dplyr::select(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size) |>
  purrr::pwalk(\(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size) {
    setup <- make_setup(
      model, dataset, c(normal = normal, defective = defective), k, max_size
    )
    write_setup(setup, file.path(setup_dir, paste0(model, "_", dataset, ".json")))
  })
```

The Platt fits, with the smallest fitted value and the distance of the
largest fitted value from 1, on the calibration images:

```{r platt-table, echo = FALSE}
saved$platt |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    min_fitted = formatC(min_fitted, format = "g", digits = 3),
    `1 - max_fitted` = formatC(1 - max_fitted, format = "g", digits = 3)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    model, dataset, n_normal, n_defective, intercept, slope, min_fitted,
    `1 - max_fitted`
  ) |>
  show()
```

All `r nrow(saved$platt)` fits converged, and `glm()` gave no warning. No
fitted value reaches 0 or 1: the fitted values lie between
`r sci(min(saved$platt$min_fitted))` and
1 - `r sci(min(1 - saved$platt$max_fitted))`.
`r if (near_bounds == 0) "No fitted value lies" else paste(near_bounds, "fitted values lie")`
within 1e-6 of 0 or 1. The clamp limits the logit, so it also limits the calibrated
probability of any raw probability. But a steep fit multiplies the logit by
its slope (up to `r fmt(steepest$slope, 1)`, for `r name_setups(steepest)`).
So at the clamp limits, `r nrow(steep)` fits (`r name_setups(steep)`) give a
calibrated probability within 1e-12 of 0 or 1.

The calibrated metrics:

```{r calibration-metrics, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
calibration_metrics <- function(model, dataset, k, result, intercept, slope,
                                ...) {
  answers <- dplyr::mutate(
    result$answers[[1]], truth = calibration_rows(dataset, k)$truth
  )
  calibrated <- dplyr::mutate(
    answers, .pred_defective = platt_apply(.pred_defective, intercept, slope)
  )
  metrics <- yardstick::metric_set(
    yardstick::roc_auc, yardstick::brier_class, yardstick::mn_log_loss
  )
  dplyr::bind_rows(
    before = metrics(answers, truth, .pred_defective, event_level = "second"),
    after = metrics(calibrated, truth, .pred_defective, event_level = "second"),
    .id = "probabilities"
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(model = model, dataset = dataset, n = nrow(answers), .before = 1)
}

calibration_summary <- calibration |>
  dplyr::left_join(platt, by = c("model", "dataset")) |>
  purrr::pmap(calibration_metrics) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
```

The table gives the AUC of the chosen setup on the calibration images, and
the Brier score and the log loss before and after Platt scaling. A lower
Brier score and a lower log loss are better. Platt scaling is strictly
increasing between the clamp limits (its slope is positive in all
`r nrow(saved$platt)` fits), so it keeps the order of the images there. Raw
probabilities below 0.005, or above 0.995, become equal. On the calibration
images, the AUC after Platt scaling
`r if (auc_same) "is the same as before for all 15 setups" else paste("changes for", name_setups(auc_changed))`.
The AUC of the test comes from the raw probabilities.

```{r calibration-table, echo = FALSE}
calibration_wide |>
  dplyr::select(-auc_after) |>
  show()
```

Platt scaling is fitted and measured on the same images, so the numbers
"after" are too good. The test images give the honest numbers.

The calibration images are new to the chosen setup (not for the pans: their
calibration rows include the grid images), so their AUC is a first check of
the choices. On most datasets, the AUC stays close to the AUC of the grid. On
the extrusion images, the AUC of Jev falls from
`r fmt(grid_auc("jev", "extrusion"))` (grid) to
`r fmt(calibration_auc("jev", "extrusion"))`. This agrees with the effect
that "Rows" describes: the choices fit the learning images better than new
images. Chance plays a part too, because 50 images give a rough AUC.

Before calibration, the probabilities of the models are often too extreme.
For gpt-6-luna on the extrusion images, the log loss is
`r fmt(pick(calibration_wide, "openai", "extrusion")$log_loss_before)`: the
model gave probabilities near 0 or 1 to images of the other class. Platt
scaling moves such probabilities toward the rates of defects, and the log
loss falls to
`r fmt(pick(calibration_wide, "openai", "extrusion")$log_loss_after)`.

For `r name_setups(separated)`, the chosen setup separates the two classes of
the calibration images fully (AUC 1). Their Platt fits stay finite, so their
Brier score and log loss "after" stay above 0. The targets of Platt pull the
probabilities a little away from 0 and 1. Where the raw probabilities are
already good, this can make the numbers "after" worse: the Brier score or the
log loss goes up for `r name_setups(worse)`.

## Folds

How much does an AUC move from one sample of images to another?
Cross-validation splits the learning images of the chosen setup into 5 folds,
10 times
(`rsample::vfold_cv()`, with the classes in the same ratio in each fold). Each
fold gives the AUC of its fifth of the images. No model is fitted, and no call
is sent: the folds use the saved probabilities of the grid.

```{r folds, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
fold_auc <- function(model, dataset, answers) {
  learning <- dplyr::filter(by_dataset[[dataset]], role == "learning")
  scored <- dplyr::mutate(answers, truth = learning$truth)
  set.seed(2026)
  rsample::vfold_cv(scored, v = 5, repeats = 10, strata = truth) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      model = model, dataset = dataset,
      auc = purrr::map_dbl(splits, \(split) {
        held_out <- rsample::assessment(split)
        yardstick::roc_auc_vec(
          held_out$truth, held_out$.pred_defective, event_level = "second"
        )
      })
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(model, dataset, id, id2, auc)
}

folds <- chosen |>
  dplyr::select(model, dataset, answers) |>
  purrr::pmap(fold_auc) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
```

```{r folds-table, echo = FALSE}
fold_summary |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    dplyr::select(saved$chosen, model, dataset, grid_auc = auc),
    by = c("model", "dataset")
  ) |>
  show()
```

```{r fold-facts, include = FALSE}
extrusion_folds <- dplyr::filter(saved$folds, dataset == "extrusion")
extrusion_sd <- mean(dplyr::filter(fold_summary, dataset == "extrusion")$sd)
other_sd <- max(dplyr::filter(fold_summary, dataset %in% c("microstructure", "textiles"))$sd)
pans_ones <- mean(dplyr::filter(saved$folds, dataset == "pan_images")$auc == 1)
staple_ones <- mean(dplyr::filter(saved$folds, dataset == "pipe_staple")$auc == 1)
```

The mean of the fold AUCs is close to the AUC of the grid, as it should be:
the folds split the same images. The spread is the useful part. On the
extrusion images, the AUC of about 18 images has a standard deviation of
about `r fmt(extrusion_sd)`, and it goes from
`r fmt(min(extrusion_folds$auc))` to `r fmt(max(extrusion_folds$auc))` over
the three models. On the microstructures and the textiles, the standard
deviation is `r fmt(other_sd)` or less. The standard deviation of an AUC falls
about as 1 / sqrt(n). So for the 92 learning images of the extrusion, it is
about `r fmt(extrusion_sd)` / sqrt(5), that is about
`r fmt(extrusion_sd / sqrt(5))`: a difference of a few hundredths between two
setups can come from chance. The pans give an AUC of 1 in
`r round(100 * pans_ones)` % of the folds, and the pipe staples in
`r round(100 * staple_ones)` %, so their folds show almost no spread.

## Test

This section is a placeholder. The test results are not in this version of
the vignette: they come from one run of the code below, after all the choices
above are fixed.

`evaluate_once()` reads the saved setup, which holds no calibrator, and
scores the test images one time. So its AUC is the AUC of the raw
probabilities. It writes the result to `path` and refuses to run again while
that file exists. So the test images give one estimate, and no choice can
use them. The Platt fit of the setup then gives the calibrated probabilities
of the test images, for the Brier score and the log loss.

```{r test, eval = FALSE}
dir.create("test")

evaluate_test <- function(model, dataset, intercept, slope, ...) {
  setup <- read_setup(file.path(setup_dir, paste0(model, "_", dataset, ".json")))
  test <- dplyr::filter(by_dataset[[dataset]], role == "test")
  result <- evaluate_once(
    setup, image = test$path, truth = test$truth,
    path = file.path("test", paste0(model, "_", dataset, ".rds"))
  )
  calibrated <- platt_apply(result$answers[[1]]$.pred_defective, intercept, slope)
  dplyr::mutate(result, model = model, dataset = dataset, calibrated = list(calibrated))
}

test_results <- chosen |>
  dplyr::select(model, dataset) |>
  dplyr::left_join(platt, by = c("model", "dataset")) |>
  purrr::pmap(evaluate_test) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
```

## Cost and time

TypeSafe, OpenAI and the Clef-Flash server report no cost, so `.cost` is
`NA`, and the reported cost below is `NA` too. All three report the input
tokens. `images` is the number of scored images: one call each. `seconds` is
the sum of the response times. The requests run in parallel (10 at a time),
so a run takes less time than this sum.

```{r cost-table, echo = FALSE}
show(cost_summary)
```

The images by step:

```{r calls-table, echo = FALSE}
show(saved$calls)
```

The wording images of gpt-6-luna are the calls of its loops. No step scored
a test image.

```{r cost-facts, include = FALSE}
per_image <- \(model_name, column) cost_summary[[column]][cost_summary$model == model_name]
token_factor <- per_image("jev", "tokens_per_image") /
  mean(c(per_image("openai", "tokens_per_image"), per_image("clef", "tokens_per_image")))
```

Jev used about `r fmt(token_factor, 1)` times the input tokens of the other
two models for the same images. The two hosted models answered in about
`r fmt(per_image("jev", "seconds_per_image"), 1)` (Jev) and
`r fmt(per_image("openai", "seconds_per_image"), 1)` (gpt-6-luna) seconds per
image. Clef-Flash ran on one GPU (NVIDIA RTX 5000 Ada, 32 GB), and it took
about `r fmt(per_image("clef", "seconds_per_image"), 1)` seconds per image, but
it costs nothing per call. Once, during the wording
step, the Clef-Flash server stopped answering. A restart of the server and a
new run with the same state files continued the step: the finished answers
came from the state files, and only the open images were sent again.

## Image size

The setup here differs slightly from the paper of the original study. This
vignette enlarges each image to 512 or 768 pixels on its longest side
(`upscale = TRUE`; the large pan images are made smaller). The paper used
1,568 pixels, with padding.
